actions.justification: Mandatory first step to fully characterize the patient's hemodynamic status, including HR, BP, RR, SpO2, and temperature, to confirm hypertensive emergency.
Mandatory assessment to confirm severely elevated blood pressure (MAP 160 mmHg) and establish baseline for treatment monitoring in suspected hypertensive emergency.
Mandatory assessment to evaluate for end-organ damage (neurological, cardiac, renal, ophthalmologic) which distinguishes hypertensive emergency from urgency and guides treatment intensity.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with markedly elevated MAP (160 mmHg), raising concern for hypertensive encephalopathy or other CNS end-organ damage. A thorough neurological assessment (GCS, focal deficits, papilledema) is essential to characterize the syndrome and guide treatment urgency.

Continuous BP monitoring is essential in hypertensive emergency to track real-time fluctuations, confirm severity, and prepare for titrated antihypertensive therapy. Helps establish a safe BP reduction target.

Neurological symptoms (severe headache, blurred vision) in the setting of hypertensive emergency warrant neurology consultation to evaluate for hypertensive encephalopathy, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), or intracranial hemorrhage before initiating treatment.

CT head is urgently needed to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, hypertensive encephalopathy, or other structural causes of severe headache and blurred vision in this hypertensive emergency. Results will guide safe BP reduction strategy.
Chest X-ray is indicated to assess for pulmonary edema or aortic widening as part of hypertensive emergency end-organ damage evaluation.
Monitoring urine output is essential to assess renal end-organ damage in hypertensive emergency, which can present with acute kidney injury.

Basic metabolic panel is essential to assess renal function, electrolytes, and glucose in this hypertensive emergency patient with elevated MAP of 160. End-organ damage assessment requires renal function labs (creatinine, BUN) which are not yet obtained.
ECG is indicated to assess for cardiac end-organ damage (LVH, ischemia, arrhythmia) in the setting of hypertensive emergency with MAP 160 and symptoms of severe headache and blurred vision.

MRI brain provides better characterization of hypertensive encephalopathy, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), or other intracranial pathology beyond what CT head provides, particularly given the blurred vision suggesting possible PRES in this hypertensive emergency.
CBC is essential to evaluate for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), thrombocytopenia, and other hematologic complications of hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage.
eGFR assessment is critical to evaluate renal end-organ damage in this hypertensive emergency patient with MAP of 160 mmHg, which is a key indicator of severity and guides treatment.
Coagulation studies are warranted to evaluate for DIC or coagulopathy associated with hypertensive emergency and to guide potential anticoagulation decisions.

Urinalysis is essential to assess for end-organ damage (proteinuria, hematuria) consistent with hypertensive emergency/crisis, helping differentiate hypertensive urgency from emergency and guiding treatment intensity.
Troponin should be ordered to evaluate for cardiac end-organ damage (hypertensive emergency with myocardial injury), given this patient's severely elevated MAP and hypertension history.

Nephrology consultation is warranted given the significantly elevated MAP (160 mmHg) with pending renal function labs (eGFR already ordered), to assist in evaluating and managing potential hypertensive nephropathy or renal crisis.

Patient has severe headache, blurred vision, and markedly elevated MAP of 160 mmHg with hypertension history, consistent with hypertensive emergency with end-organ involvement (neurological symptoms). IV labetalol is a first-line agent for hypertensive emergency to safely reduce BP by ~25% in first hour. Assessment and imaging are already completed.

Hypertensive emergency with neurological symptoms (severe headache, blurred vision) and MAP 160 requires ICU-level monitoring for continuous BP management, titration of IV antihypertensives, and monitoring for further end-organ damage.
